title: Franklin's Lost Expedition
intro: HMS Erebus and HMS Terror left England in 1845 under Captain Sir John Franklin, with 129 officers and men, to traverse the last unnavigated sections of the Northwest Passage in the Canadian Arctic. Both ships became icebound in Victoria Strait near King William Island.
ending: The ships were abandoned in April 1848 and the survivors, led by Francis Crozier, set out for the Canadian mainland and disappeared. Later searchers, Inuit testimony and the finding of the wrecks in 2014 and 2016 told what became of them.

stops.text: The expedition sailed from Greenhithe, Kent, on the morning of 19 May 1845, with a crew of 24 officers and 110 men aboard Erebus and Terror.
stops.quote: The expedition set sail from Greenhithe, Kent, on the morning of 19 May 1845, with a crew of 24 officers and 110 men.

stops.text: The ships stopped briefly at Stromness in the Orkney Islands to take on fresh water. From there they sailed to Greenland with HMS Rattler and the transport Barretto Junior, a passage of 30 days.
stops.quote: The ships stopped briefly to take aboard fresh water in Stromness, Orkney Islands, in northern Scotland.

stops.text: At the Whalefish Islands in Disko Bay ten oxen carried on Barretto Junior were slaughtered for fresh meat, and the crews wrote their last letters home. Five men were sent home sick, which left 129 men.
stops.quote: At the Whalefish Islands in Disko Bay, on the west coast of Greenland, ten oxen carried on Barretto Junior were slaughtered for fresh meat which was transferred to Erebus and Terror.

legs.title: Into the ice and the march south

stops.text: Franklin's men spent the winter of 1845–46 on Beechey Island. Three crew members died there and were buried.
stops.quote: Franklin's men spent the winter of 1845–46 on Beechey Island, where three crew members died and were buried.

stops.text: After travelling down Peel Sound through the summer, Terror and Erebus became trapped in ice off King William Island. They are thought never to have sailed again. Franklin died on 11 June 1847, according to the Victory Point Note.
stops.quote: After travelling down Peel Sound through the summer of 1846, Terror and Erebus became trapped in ice off King William Island in September 1846 and are thought never to have sailed again.

stops.text: The ships were deserted on 22 April 1848. Crozier and Fitzjames recorded that 105 men had landed, that 9 officers and 15 men had died, and that they would start for the Back River on 26 April.
stops.quote: According to the second part of the Victory Point Note dated 25 April 1848 and signed by Fitzjames and Crozier, the crew had wintered off King William Island in 1846–47 and 1847–48 and Franklin had died on 11 June 1847.

stops.text: From archaeological finds it is believed that all the remaining crew died on the 400 km march to the Back River, most on the island. Thirty or forty men reached the northern coast of the mainland before dying.
stops.quote: The Schwatka expedition found no remnants of the Franklin expedition south of a place now known as Starvation Cove on the Adelaide Peninsula.

stops.text: John Rae met an Inuk near Pelly Bay, who told him of 35 to 40 white men who had died of starvation near the mouth of the Back River. Other Inuit confirmed this, with reports of cannibalism among the dying sailors.
stops.quote: Rae met an Inuk near Pelly Bay (now Kugaaruk, Nunavut) on 21 April 1854, who told him of a party of 35 to 40 white men who had died of starvation near the mouth of the Back River.

stops.text: Lieutenant William Hobson's sled party found the Victory Point Note in a cairn on the north-western coast of King William Island. It told of the abandonment of the ships, Franklin's death and the march south.
stops.quote: On 5 May, the party led by Lieutenant William Hobson discovered the Victory Point Note, which detailed the abandonment of Erebus and Terror, death of Franklin and other crew members, and the decision by the survivors to march south to the mainland.

stops.place: NgLj-2, western shore of King William Island
stops.text: Archaeologists excavated nearly 400 bones and fragments on the island's western shore. Many bore cut marks consistent with de-fleshing, and it is now generally accepted that some of Franklin's men resorted to cannibalism.
stops.quote: In 1993, a team of archaeologists and forensic anthropologists returned to the site, which they referenced as "NgLj-2", on the western shores of King William Island, to excavate these remains.

stops.text: A Canadian search team located Erebus in about 11 m of water in Wilmot and Crampton Bay, west of O'Reilly Island. The ship was preserved in good condition.
stops.quote: On 9 September 2014, the expedition announced that on 7 September it had located one of Franklin's two ships.

stops.text: The Arctic Research Foundation announced that it had found the wreck of Terror in Terror Bay, south of King William Island, at a depth of 24 m.
stops.quote: On 12 September 2016, it was announced that the Arctic Research Foundation expedition had found the wreck of HMS Terror to the south of King William Island in Terror Bay

notes: No stop matches places.tsv (orkney is the region, not Stromness). Left out: Baffin Bay (a bay; the whalers met the ships there in late July 1845), Wellington Channel, Cornwallis Island and Peel Sound (channels), Montreal Island (Anderson's 1855 find, no usable quote for a point), Erebus Bay/boat place (no own article named). Wp titles to check: Whalefish Islands, Starvation Cove, Terror Bay, O'Reilly Island may lack articles; Pelly Bay uses Kugaaruk. Stops with date null: the article gives no date for them. Beechey Island date is the winter, year 1845. Franklin's death (11 June 1847) and the 22 April abandonment come from the Victory Point Note as quoted in the article. The article says the first 1847 message wrongly dates the Beechey wintering. Woodman's argument that many survived past 1848 is in the article but not used. NgLj-2: later reviews doubt its identity with the boat place; the stop keeps the article's 1993 excavation. Dates of the Erebus find (7 September) and announcement (9 September) both given.
